The model does not say whether a defect that turns a transient host fault into a lasting non-stop refusal, one that outlasts the fault without a wrong hash, proof or directory, falls under the host-fault exclusion or under the R4 recovery duty. reviewer_reason: The facts reproduce (exit 1 on rerun; store_machine calls only machine:store). But O2 says 'guarantees a stored directory only when it was synced', and cm.h ~600 says stored files are 'durable only after cm_sync_stored()'. reviewer_severity: Out of scope / Low (preferred: an unsynced --store directory is not guaranteed by O2, and losing it needs a reload after a stop, which is excluded; at most the manual's template sections leave out a sync step). Medium under the alternative reading that 'tools must follow them' requires every directory a tool writes to be left guaranteed (stand-in rule for a Support component).
gap: Section 5 says 'The tools ... must follow' O1/O2, but it does not say whether a tool that writes a stored directory meant for later reuse (here, a template made with --store) must leave it guaranteed by syncing it, or only must never resume from an unguaranteed one. The text also does not say whether a power loss after a clean exit is a 'stop' of the writing process. The test's Part A asserts the first reading. Part B asserts that an unguaranteed directory reloads, which section 8 excludes. The PRT player clones the template and syncs the clone (prt.lua:2751-2752), so its checkpoints are guaranteed either way.

reviewer_reason: Re-ran the test: exit 1, deterministic. The manual says uarch code "has access to the entire state", and it draws that state as a 64-bit tree whose unmapped space is "implicitly filled with zeros". "In addition to ... all memory ranges and devices" sets a minimum and does not list the whole map. The uarch reaches devices through their shadows. All paths agree, so R3's "memory map does not allow" never applies. The state is unreachable. A fix to the docs would leave the test failing.
reviewer_severity: Low (best-supported reading) / High for the hole loads if the manual's uarch map is read as exhaustive
gap: R3 defines a trap as 'an access that its memory map does not allow', but neither THREAT_MODEL nor the manual defines the uarch memory map for loads exhaustively. The manual's 'access to the entire state' together with its zero-filled 64-bit state tree supports reads anywhere. Reading 'In addition to ... all memory ranges and devices ... private 2MiB' as an exhaustive map would make hole loads traps, and the verifiers' acceptance would then be High. The EVM revert at 0xfffffffffffffff8 is a separate issue, already R1-R10-2.

reviewer_reason: Facts hold: run.sh exits 1 twice (5 mismatches). store writes stale m_c, but init_processor loads registers from config only if backing_store.newly_created(), and stored configs always name the processor file, so no hash or transition reads them; R2 holds. Medium case 'leaves ... a stored directory inconsistent with the machine's contents (R9)' covers hash data, not these fields, and store is on-path. Not 'security-relevant'; Low.
gap: Two things are unclear. First, whether the Medium case 'stored directory inconsistent with the machine's contents (R9)' covers non-hash metadata that no load path reads, here config.json register fields. Second, what makes a manual contradiction 'security-relevant' when it concerns inert fields. The rating would be higher if a production on-path reader used these fields, or if load or re-instantiation took registers from them; neither happens. The fix may also be a manual change, in which case the test would keep failing.

reviewer_reason: The test exits 1 on every run, for the reason claimed. The section 3 support clause applies: "Medium when it would rate High or Critical in the role the component stands in for". But no in-scope verifier shares the flaw. Dave fixes the template hash on-chain and delivers inputs through cmio. gap: The model says "a proof verifier accepts a node that the committed tree does not hold" (section 1), and the emulator provides "Merkle proofs of any aligned node" (section 3). But section 2 lists node-index referee parameters only for computation-hash proofs and A5 extraction proofs. It does not say whether a verifier for the manual's documented template instantiation by NVRAM splicing, or for result extraction from a halted machine's NVRAM, is an in-scope stood-in role. One reading gives Low: no deployment does this, and the intro limits scope to PRT. The deciding fact: is any deployed or in-scope referee component (Dave, the doc/recipes PRT referee model) instantiating templates by splicing, or accepting non-A5 node proofs, without binding root, address and size? reviewer_reason: Test exits 1 deterministically (3 reruns): CannotAdvanceTimedOutClock at match 3, response 22. Facts verified. Section 4 says "history that its policy treats as final", and "A reorganization deeper than that" lets the operator choose its depth. R4 makes the operator itself "submit its transactions within the dispute clocks". A7 sizes the clocks "at the worst-case costs of R12", not for finality. A LAG-4 control wins. No rule is broken.
reviewer_severity: Low (preferred: an operator dispute policy shallower than G is an allowed "final" policy, and with it the honest claim wins) / Medium (section 3 support clause) or Critical (A7, as in R1-A7-1), if every deployment must let the operator answer from Ethereum-finalized history
gap: Section 4 does not say what "final" means. "History that its policy treats as final, such as finalized blocks" could mean any confirmation depth the operator picks, or the chain's real finality. The threat model never says whether a deployment's per-response clock must cover the chain's finality delay. Dave's dimensioning.md says a joined match's responses "read latest". If finality is required, this finding becomes Medium or Critical, and section 3's support clause on response time decides which.

reviewer_reason: A5 defines acceptance as "through a proof that authenticates a hash as a leaf". The manual's normative referee "accepts output proofs against that root". validateOutput accepts this voucher. Only executing it fails. No rule bounds that execution cost. The "honest proof or transaction" clause (R12: "transaction the honest operator sends") does not cover a user's executeOutput. The AUDIT row says "output validation" and does not mention execution. Test exits 1 deterministically, as claimed.
reviewer_severity: Low (preferred: A5 acceptance = proof validation) / Critical (if A5's 'accepts' includes executing a voucher within the chain's per-transaction limits)
gap: The model never says whether A5's 'accepts' covers executing a voucher, or whether outputs need a size bound like A3's bound on inputs. libcmt allows outputs up to the 2 MiB tx buffer. The model also does not fix the chain's per-transaction limit; the test assumes Ethereum mainnet EIP-7825 (2^24). Settling it: say whether output execution within per-transaction limits is a referee obligation (Critical), or only proof validation is (Low).

Under the narrow reading, an unhashed padded config.json makes adoption cost unbounded relative to the machine: Critical at step 4 via R12/R4 on 'Obtaining its valid template', or High if the template counts as declinable data from others.
